propositions.text: The appellants appealed a Federal Court decision dismissing judicial review of a Minister's decision.
propositions.quote: The appellants have appealed a decision of the Federal Court (2021 FC 1125 per Kane J.) dismissing an application for judicial review of a decision of the Minister of Employment, Workforce, and Labour (the Minister).

propositions.text: The respondent moves to strike the appeal as moot.
propositions.quote: The respondent has brought a motion to strike the appeal on the ground that it is moot.

propositions.text: The appellants oppose the motion to strike the appeal as moot.
propositions.quote: The appellants oppose the motion.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants appealed a Federal Court decision; the respondent moves to strike the appeal as moot, opposed by the appellants.

propositions.text: The Minister's decision added a requirement to attest respect for human rights, including reproductive rights, in the 2018 CSJ funding application.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s impugned decision (the Decision) was “to add to the application for funding under the [2018] Canada Summer Jobs (“CSJ”) program … the requirement that the applicants attest” that “the job [for which funding was sought] and the organization’s core mandate respect individual human rights in Canada, including the values underlying the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms as well as other rights.” The attestation made specific reference to reproductive rights and the Applicant Guide for the 2018 CSJ program explained that human rights include reproductive rights and the right to access safe and legal abortions.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister added a requirement to attest respect for human rights, including reproductive rights, in the 2018 CSJ funding application.

propositions.text: TRTL did not make the attestation but enclosed a letter objecting to it and offered an alternative attestation.
propositions.quote: In its application for funding under the 2018 CSJ program, the appellant, Right to Life Association of Toronto and Area (TRTL), did not make the attestation. Rather, it enclosed a letter objecting to it, asserting the Minister did not have the jurisdiction to compel TRTL to make a statement that conflicts with its conscience rights or to compel speech. It offered an alternative attestation.

propositions.text: The Minister declined to consider TRTL’s application because it was incomplete without the required attestation.
propositions.quote: The Minister declined to consider TRTL’s application because it was incomplete: TRTL had not made the required attestation.

propositions.text: TRTL did not receive funding in 2018; Alleyne is former president and Battista hoped to be employed by TRTL.
propositions.quote: As a result, TRTL did not receive any funding in 2018. The appellant, Blaise Alleyne, is a former president of TRTL and the appellant, Matthew Battista, is a student who hoped to be employed by TRTL in the summer of 2018.

paragraphs.summary: TRTL did not make the attestation, objected, offered alternative; Minister declined application; TRTL got no funding; Alleyne and Battista are appellants.

propositions.text: Appellants sought judicial review declaring the Decision infringed Charter rights, was ultra vires, bad faith, and mandamus ordering funding.
propositions.quote: The appellants sought judicial review of the Decision, a declaration that the Decision infringed provisions in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms [Charter], a declaration the Decision was ultra vires, made in bad faith and for an improper purpose, and an order in the nature of mandamus that the TRTL be awarded the 2018 CSJ program funds that it would have been awarded had its application been considered without regard to the attestation.

propositions.text: Appellants did not seek judicial review of the refusal to consider TRTL’s application or alternative attestation.
propositions.quote: The appellants did not seek judicial review of the decision not to review TRTL’s application and thereby deny it funding.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants sought judicial review declaring the Decision infringed Charter rights and mandamus for funding; did not seek review of refusal to consider application.

propositions.text: Federal Court found the Decision reasonable, not ultra vires, not bad faith or improper purpose.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court decided that the Decision was reasonable, was not ultra vires the Department of Employment and Social Development Act, S.C. 2005, c. 34, [DESDA] under which it was established, and was not made in bad faith or for an improper purpose.

propositions.text: Federal Court found TRTL’s section 15 Charter rights not engaged; section 2(a) and 2(b) engaged but justified under section 1 as minimal limitation.
propositions.quote: It also concluded that TRTL’s section 15 Charter rights were not engaged and, while its section 2(a) and section 2(b) Charter freedoms were engaged, the limitation on those freedoms was justified under section 1, most particularly because it was minimal: “a one-time impact on potential—not certain—funding in 2018”.

propositions.text: Federal Court viewed limitation as proportionate balancing of freedoms and program objectives.
propositions.quote: In the Federal Court’s view, the limitation reflected a proportionate balancing of those freedoms and the objectives of the DESDA and the 2018 CSJ program.

propositions.text: Federal Court found Alleyne had standing but Battista did not.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court also decided that while Mr. Alleyne, as the face of TRTL and the person required to sign the application on its behalf, had standing, Mr. Battista did not.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court found Decision reasonable, not ultra vires, no bad faith; TRTL’s s.15 rights not engaged; s.2 rights limited but justified; Alleyne had standing, Battista did not.

propositions.text: Appellants assert Federal Court erred on s.15 Charter rights, s.2 infringements, closed mind, and Battista’s standing.
propositions.quote: In their appeal, the appellants assert that the Federal Court erred in concluding that their section 15 Charter rights were not violated, that the infringements under section 2 were proportionately balanced, and that the Minister did not make the Decision with a closed mind. They also assert that the Federal Court erred in concluding Mr. Battista had no standing.

propositions.text: Steps to set appeal for hearing are complete.
propositions.quote: The steps required to set the appeal down for hearing are complete.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants assert Federal Court erred on Charter rights and standing; appeal ready for hearing.

propositions.text: Respondent moves to strike appeal as moot, citing removal of attestation and program conclusion.
propositions.quote: The respondent now moves to strike the appeal because it is moot. The respondent says there is no longer a live controversy between the parties. In particular, says the respondent, the impugned attestation was removed from the 2019 application, a fact that the appellants do not dispute and that was noted in Redeemer University College v. Canada (Employment, Workforce Development and Labour), 2021 FC 686, 334 A.C.W.S. (3d) 679 at para. 8 [Redeemer University]. Moreover, says the respondent, the 2018 CSJ program is concluded and available funding has been disbursed.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent moves to strike appeal as moot due to attestation removal and program conclusion.

propositions.text: Appellants argue mootness should not be raised first time on appeal.
propositions.quote: The appellants submit that the Court should not entertain the respondent’s motion because the respondent could have raised mootness earlier and should not be permitted to raise this “new issue” for the first time on appeal.

propositions.text: Mootness may be raised at any time, including by the Court itself.
propositions.quote: While the desirability of addressing mootness at an early stage is obvious, mootness may be raised at any time. It may be raised by the Court if the parties do not raise it: Canadian Union of Public Employees (Air Canada Component) v. Air Canada, 2021 FCA 67, [2021] F.C.J. No 286 (Q.L.) [CUPE]; Hakizimana v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2022 FCA 33, 87 Imm. L.R. (4th) 175 [Hakizimana].

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue mootness raised too late; court holds mootness may be raised anytime, even by court itself.

propositions.text: First question is whether the appeal is moot; if so, whether to exercise discretion to hear it per Borowski factors.
propositions.quote: Thus, the first question to answer is whether the appeal is moot. If it is, then this Court must decide whether it will nevertheless exercise its discretion to hear the appeal, having regard to the factors from Borowski v. Canada, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342, 57 D.L.R. (4th) 231 [Borowski].

paragraphs.summary: Court must decide if appeal is moot and if it should hear it using Borowski factors.

propositions.text: Judicial review concerned Decision adding attestation to 2018 CSJ application, not refusal to consider TRTL’s application or alternative attestation.
propositions.quote: Here, the subject of the judicial review was the Decision to add the attestation to the application under the 2018 CSJ program. It was not a judicial review of the decision not to consider TRTL’s application for funding under that program in the absence of the attestation, or of the refusal to consider or accept TRTL’s alternative attestation.

paragraphs.summary: Judicial review concerned Decision adding attestation, not refusal to consider TRTL’s application or alternative attestation.

propositions.text: 2018 CSJ program ended and attestation removed from 2019 application; review of Decision serves no useful purpose.
propositions.quote: The 2018 CSJ program has ended and the attestation was removed from the application form for the 2019 CSJ program year. Thus, a review of the reasonableness of the Decision to add the attestation to the 2018 application will not serve a useful purpose; the Decision has been overtaken by subsequent events.

paragraphs.summary: 2018 program ended and attestation removed; review of Decision serves no useful purpose.

propositions.text: Appellants say appeal not moot because declaration of Charter breach is live controversy, citing Trang 2005.
propositions.quote: The appellants say the appeal is not moot because they seek a declaration of a Charter breach and that constitutes a live controversy, citing Trang v. Alberta (Edmonton Remand Centre), 2005 ABCA 66, 363 A.R. 167 at para. 5 [Trang 2005]. TRTL concedes that “in the case at bar … the core remedy sought is a declaration that the Respondent breached the Appellants’ Charter rights in 2018”.

propositions.text: Court may make binding declaration but whether to do so depends on circumstances.
propositions.quote: I acknowledge that the Court may make a binding declaration and that such a declaration can be an adequate remedy, but whether the Court will make a declaration depends on the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants say declaration of Charter breach keeps appeal live; court says declaration depends on circumstances.

propositions.text: Declaration of Charter breach may only be granted if it has practical utility and settles a live controversy.
propositions.quote: A declaration that the Charter was breached may, but does not always, constitute a live controversy. A declaration may be granted only if it will have practical utility, that is, if it will settle a “live controversy” between the parties: Daniels v. Canada (Indian Affairs and Northern Development), 2016 SCC 12, [2016] 1 S.C.R. 99 at para. 11; Solosky v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 821, 105 D.L.R. (3d) 745; Income Security Advocacy Centre v. Mette, 2016 FCA 167, [2016] F.C.J. No. 587 (Q.L.) at para. 6.

paragraphs.summary: Declaration of Charter breach granted only if it has practical utility and settles live controversy.

propositions.text: A declaration that Charter rights were violated for 2018 attestation would have no practical utility now.
propositions.quote: Here, were the appellants successful on appeal, a declaration that Charter rights were violated by the inclusion of the attestation in the application form for a program that is spent, would serve no practical utility and would not resolve any live controversy.

propositions.text: Future similar attestation requirements can be challenged then; this decision likely of no use in future cases.
propositions.quote: If, in the future, a funding program contains a similar attestation requirement, it can be challenged at that time. And, of course, the challenge necessarily would depend on the type of attestation requirement and the reasons behind it. There is a good chance that a decision in this case on these particular facts would be of no use in that later case.

paragraphs.summary: Declaration on 2018 attestation would have no practical utility; future similar cases can be challenged then.

propositions.text: Declarations may not be granted if dispute is academic or has no practical effect, per Trang 2007.
propositions.quote: Indeed, in the sequel to Trang 2005, the Alberta Court of Appeal stated that “[d]eclarations may not be granted where the dispute has become academic, or will have no practical effect in resolving any remaining issues between the parties”: Trang v. Alberta (Edmonton Remand Centre), 2007 ABCA 263, 412 A.R. 215, at para. 15, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 32310 (21 February, 2008), [Trang 2007]. That decision overturned the lower court’s decision to grant a declaration of a breach of Charter rights, explaining why declarations rarely will be granted if they will have no practical effect on the rights of the parties: Trang 2007 at paras. 13-25.

paragraphs.summary: Declarations may not be granted if dispute is academic or has no practical effect, per Trang 2007.

propositions.text: Utility of declaration depends on other available remedies; here, only mandamus could provide practical relief.
propositions.quote: One relevant consideration to the utility of a declaration is the other remedies, if any, that would be available if the declaration is made. In this appeal, unless this Court is prepared to issue mandamus and order the Minister to process TRTL’s 2018 CSJ program application and provide it with the funds it would have received had its application been processed, none of the relief claimed in the application for judicial review or the notice of appeal in this Court is of any practical utility.

paragraphs.summary: Declaration's utility depends on other remedies; only mandamus could provide practical relief here.

propositions.text: Mandamus is discretionary and requires satisfying eight criteria or severe maladministration.
propositions.quote: Mandamus is a discretionary remedy that may be granted where the applicant satisfies the eight criteria set out by this Court in Apotex Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 F.C. 742, 162 N.R. 177 (F.C.A.), aff’d [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1100, 176 N.R. 1, or in cases of severe maladministration as described in cases such as Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) v. LeBon, 2013 FCA 55, 444 N.R. 93 at para. 14 and D'Errico v. Canada (Attorney General), 2014 FCA 95, 459 N.R. 167 at paras. 16-21 [D’Errico].

propositions.text: Appellants have not addressed mandamus criteria; record shows no basis for mandamus; this supports view declaration has no practical utility.
propositions.quote: The appellants have not addressed these criteria in their application for judicial review, their notice of appeal, their memorandum of fact and law, or their materials on this motion. In any event, the record discloses no basis for mandamus. This augments my view that a declaration that Charter rights were violated would serve no practical utility.

paragraphs.summary: Mandamus requires criteria; appellants did not address them; no basis found; declaration lacks practical utility.

propositions.text: Even if TRTL’s 2018 application was processed, funding was not certain due to oversubscription and priorities.
propositions.quote: I also observe that even if TRTL’s 2018 application had been processed, TRTL may not have received any funding under the 2018 CSJ program. The 2018 CSJ program, like the CSJ program in other years, was oversubscribed. Because demand exceeds available funding, each year the Minister establishes national priorities and eligibility criteria for the CSJ program. As the Federal Court observed, under the 2018 CSJ program, “given other eligibility criteria and the stated priorities and target population, funding was not a certainty” and those other criteria and priorities “do not appear to reflect TRTL’s mandate or activities.”

propositions.text: Mandamus granted only where outcome on merits is foregone conclusion, absent extreme maladministration.
propositions.quote: Absent extreme maladministration, courts grant mandamus “only where the outcome on the merits is a foregone conclusion – in other words the evidence can lead only to one result”: D’Errico at para 16; Doyle v. Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FCA 56, 2022 A.C.W.S. 740.

paragraphs.summary: Funding was not certain due to oversubscription; mandamus granted only if outcome is foregone conclusion.

propositions.text: Claim for mandamus insufficient to render appeal not moot; appeal is moot.
propositions.quote: Thus, in my view, the claim for mandamus is not sufficient to render this appeal not moot. Indeed, I am satisfied it is moot.

paragraphs.summary: Mandamus claim insufficient; appeal is moot.

propositions.text: Court must consider whether to hear moot appeal using Borowski factors: adversarial context, practical utility, and proper role.
propositions.quote: I now turn to consider whether the Court should nevertheless hear the appeal, having regard to the following factors from Borowski at 358-363: (i) the absence or presence of an adversarial context; (ii) whether there is any practical utility in deciding the matter or if it is a waste of judicial resources; and (iii) whether the Court would be exceeding its proper role by making law in the abstract, a task that is reserved for Parliament. See also CUPE at para. 9. No one factor is determinative.

paragraphs.summary: Court considers whether to hear moot appeal using Borowski factors: adversarial context, utility, and proper role.

propositions.text: There is an adversarial context with fully argued issues and submissions from two interveners before the Federal Court
propositions.quote: I agree with the parties that there is an adversarial context. The issues were fully argued before the Federal Court, which also had the benefit of submissions from two interveners.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds there was an adversarial context with fully argued issues and interveners' submissions before the Federal Court.

propositions.text: The 2018 CSJ program is expired and the impugned attestation was removed in 2019
propositions.quote: The 2018 CSJ program is expired. The impugned attestation was removed from the application in 2019.

propositions.text: Moot appeals should not be heard based on mere speculation the same issue may arise again
propositions.quote: The mere fact that the same issue may arise again—and there is no suggestion it will—does not justify hearing a moot appeal: Hakizimana at para. 22.

propositions.text: The court is not convinced future occurrences of the issue would evade court review
propositions.quote: I am not convinced that if the same issue does arise in the future, it is evasive of court review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the program expired, moot appeals on speculation are unjustified, and future issues are not evasive of review.

propositions.text: Judicial review can be an effective remedy for Charter breaches and may proceed more quickly than damages actions
propositions.quote: I agree a judicial review can be an effective remedy for Charter breaches, in part because it may proceed more quickly than an action for damages and has the potential to cause the decision-maker to respond quickly and change its conduct.

propositions.text: The CSJ application form was changed after 2018
propositions.quote: In fact, as noted, the application form for the CSJ program was changed after 2018.

propositions.text: Effectiveness of judicial review does not mean this appeal should be heard or a declaration made on past circumstances
propositions.quote: But the fact that it can be an effective remedy does not mean a particular judicial review, or an appeal of a judicial review decision, should be heard.

propositions.text: Deciding on issues without an existing factual matrix is inappropriate if application process changes yearly
propositions.quote: If, as the appellants contend, the application process is amended every year, this Court would be deciding an issue in the absence of an existing factual matrix: Hakizimana at para. 19.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds judicial review effective but this appeal should not be heard due to changed application forms and lack of current factual matrix.

propositions.text: The Court should hear the appeal because the Federal Court decision will be binding precedent immune from appellate review
propositions.quote: The appellants also assert that this Court should hear the appeal because, if it does not, the decision of the Federal Court below will be binding precedent immune from appellate review.

propositions.text: Jurisprudential interest alone is insufficient to sustain a moot appeal
propositions.quote: This proposition suggests the appellants’ interest in the appeal is jurisprudential, which is insufficient to sustain an otherwise moot appeal: CUPE at para. 7.

propositions.text: Such an argument could be made in any moot appeal and cannot alone determine hearing
propositions.quote: Although perhaps a relevant consideration, it cannot be determinative on its own for, if it were, the doctrine of mootness would be significantly weakened.

propositions.text: A decision here may have no jurisprudential impact as future programs may differ
propositions.quote: In any event, as I have explained above, a decision in this case may have no jurisprudential impact, as future programs may be based on different criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the appeal should be heard to avoid binding precedent; the court rejects this as insufficient and notes future programs may differ.

propositions.text: Raising a constitutional question alone does not justify hearing an appeal unless social cost of uncertainty outweighs judicial economy
propositions.quote: As previously observed by this Court, raising a constitutional question is not sufficient to justify hearing the appeal unless it can be demonstrated that the social cost of legal uncertainty outweighs the economy of judicial resources;

propositions.text: This Court has refused to rule on theoretical questions despite their importance
propositions.quote: on many occasions, this Court has refused to rule on questions that have become theoretical despite the importance they could assume: Abel v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FCA 131, [2021] A.C.F. No. 668 at para. 22.

propositions.text: The court is not convinced social cost here outweighs judicial economy
propositions.quote: Given the nature of the CSJ program and the issues raised on this appeal, I am not convinced that the social cost here outweighs the economy of judicial resources.

paragraphs.summary: The court states constitutional questions alone do not justify hearing appeals unless social cost outweighs judicial economy; here it does not.

propositions.text: Hearing the appeal would be law-making in the abstract with no practical consequences
propositions.quote: In my view, it would. At this stage, since the impugned attestation has been removed from the application, to consider the issues on appeal “in a case with no practical consequences, just to create a legal precedent, would be a form of law-making for the sake of law-making [and that] is not our proper task”: CUPE at para. 13.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds hearing the appeal would be abstract law-making without practical consequences, which is improper.

propositions.text: This Court should not hear this appeal
propositions.quote: Thus, in my view, this Court should not hear this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes it should not hear the appeal.

propositions.text: The appeal is moot and the Court should not exercise discretion to hear it
propositions.quote: This appeal is moot and the Court should not exercise its discretion to hear it.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the appeal is moot and should not be heard.

propositions.text: The respondent seeks costs of $800 for this motion
propositions.quote: The respondent seeks costs of $800 for this motion.

propositions.text: The appellants were silent on the issue of costs
propositions.quote: The appellants were silent on the issue of costs.

propositions.text: The court would not award costs and notes respondent should have brought motion sooner
propositions.quote: In my discretion, I would not award any costs. Although successful, the respondent should have brought this motion far sooner.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent seeks costs; appellants silent; court declines costs and notes respondent delayed bringing motion.

propositions.text: The respondent was originally named as Minister but proper respondent is Attorney General of Canada under Federal Court Rules
propositions.quote: The respondent was originally named as the “Canada (Minister of Employment, Workforce, and Labour)”. Under Rule 303 of the Federal Court Rules S.O.R./98-106, the proper respondent in these circumstances is the Attorney General of Canada.

propositions.text: This change has no bearing on the outcome and is only a matter of form
propositions.quote: This has no bearing on the outcome of this motion and is only a matter of form.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the proper respondent is Attorney General of Canada; this is a formality with no outcome effect.

propositions.text: The style of cause is amended to reflect Attorney General as respondent, motion to strike appeal for mootness granted, appeal dismissed without costs
propositions.quote: Accordingly, I would amend the style of cause to reflect the Attorney General of Canada as the sole respondent, grant the motion to strike the appeal for mootness, and dismiss the appeal without costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders style amended, motion to strike appeal granted, and appeal dismissed without costs.
